safetyNote: • Seattle is hilly and often rainy. Wear good shoes, bring a jacket, and take care on wet pavement and steep streets.

stops.name: Space Needle
stops.teaser: A flying saucer on a tripod, built in about 8 months.
stops.map: Space Needle, 400 Broad St, Seattle, WA
stops.clue: Go to Seattle Center and look up at the tall tower with a saucer-shaped top.
stops.safety: Seattle Center is busy. Stay on walkways and crossings, and note that the observation deck needs a ticket. Check the weather first.

story: Construction began on April 17, 1961. The tower opened on April 21, 1962 for the 1962 World's Fair, called Century 21. It stands 605 feet tall to the top of the spire.

Edward E. Carlson's concept was a giant tethered balloon, sketched on a napkin. John Graham's concept was a flying saucer holding the restaurant and observation deck. Victor Steinbrueck added the hourglass profile and tripod design.
The revolving restaurant stopped turning on March 27, 1964, after the Alaska earthquake. A $100 million renovation reopened in August 2018, with a revolving glass floor called the Loupe.
stops.fact: The original paint names were Orbital Olive, Astronaut White, Re-entry Red and Galaxy Gold.
stops.disputed: Nothing big is disputed. The most common mistake is thinking the restaurant has always rotated.

claims.t: The Space Needle was built for the 1962 World's Fair.
claims.why: Wikipedia: it opened April 21, 1962 for the Century 21 Exposition.

claims.t: The Space Needle's restaurant has rotated nonstop since 1962.
claims.why: It stopped rotating on March 27, 1964, after the Alaska earthquake.

spot.q: The 1961 photo shows the tower going up. Whose idea was a flying saucer holding the restaurant and observation deck?
spot.why: John Graham's concept was the flying saucer. Edward E. Carlson sketched a tethered balloon on a napkin, and Victor Steinbrueck added the hourglass profile and tripod design.

stops.name: Pike Place Market
stops.teaser: A market where fish fly and a bronze pig keeps the money.
stops.map: Pike Place Market, 85 Pike St, Seattle, WA
stops.clue: Walk to the market on Pike Place near the waterfront. Find the big bronze pig near the "Public Market Center" sign.
stops.safety: The market is very crowded. Watch for delivery carts, wet floors near fish counters, and traffic on the cobbled street.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.hint: Check the plaque near the statue.
q.verify: Wikipedia says the 550-pound bronze piggy bank is named Rachel. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: The early market
then.line: Vendors gathering on Pike Place around the time the market opened in 1907.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The Public Market sign
now.line: The Public Market Center sign at Pike Place Market. Photo from 2017.

story: Pike Place Market opened on August 17, 1907. Its goal was to let consumers "Meet the Producer." Frank Goodwin and his brothers developed most of the core buildings and kept the decoration minimal so the focus stayed on products and low prices.
In 1971, voters passed a historic preservation initiative on November 2 by a 2-to-1 margin. It created a historic district and kept the market in public hands.
Rachel is a 550-pound bronze piggy bank by Georgia Gerber, in place since 1986. It collects roughly $6,000 to $9,000 a year for the Market Foundation's social services.
stops.fact: Employees throw fish, such as three-foot salmon, across the counter instead of handing them over.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia calls it "one of the older continuously operated public farmers' markets," not the oldest, so be wary of bigger claims.

claims.t: The Starbucks at Pike Place Market is still in its original 1971 location.
claims.why: The first Starbucks opened in 1971 at 2000 Western Avenue and moved in 1977 to 1912 Pike Place.

spot.q: The early photo shows vendors on Pike Place. What did voters do for the Market in 1971?
options: Turned it into a private company
Created a historic district and kept the market in public hands
spot.why: On November 2, 1971, voters passed a preservation initiative by a 2-to-1 margin. It created a historic district and kept the market in public hands.

stops.name: Smith Tower
stops.teaser: A skyscraper built by a typewriter fortune.
stops.clue: Go to Pioneer Square and look for the white terra-cotta tower with a pointed roof.
stops.safety: Pioneer Square sidewalks are busy and uneven. Watch for traffic and stay on crossings.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Look at the very top of the tower. What shape is the roof?
q.verify: Sources describe the tower topped by a pyramid. Check on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.line: Smith Tower with Mount Rainier behind it, in 1914.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The tower today
now.line: Smith Tower rising over Pioneer Square. Photo from 2007.

story: Smith Tower was completed in 1914 and opened to the public on July 4, 1914. It is named for Lyman Cornelius Smith, a New York industrialist known for firearms and typewriters. He died in 1910, before construction began, and his son Burns Lyman Smith oversaw it. Gaggin & Gaggin of Syracuse, New York designed it.
It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until the Kansas City Power & Light Building was finished in 1931.

On the top floor, the Chinese Room has a carved teak ceiling and blackwood furniture said to be furnished by Empress Cixi. The tower kept elevator operators longer than most West Coast buildings. Elevators were automated starting in 2017.
stops.fact: The tower was one of the last on the West Coast to use elevator operators.
stops.disputed: The tower's height is quoted differently in different sources, and the Wishing Chair story is a legend.

claims.t: Smith Tower was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River when it was finished.
claims.why: Wikipedia: it held that title until 1931.

claims.t: Sitting in the Wishing Chair in the Chinese Room will bring marriage within a year.
claims.why: It is a legend. Smith's daughter married in the room, but nobody can prove the chair works.

spot.q: In 1914 Smith Tower was a record-setter. Which record is true?
options: It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until 1931
It was the tallest building in North America until 1931
It was the tallest wooden building in the world
It was the tallest building in the world until 1931
spot.why: It was the tallest building west of the Mississippi River until the Kansas City Power & Light Building was finished in 1931.

stops.name: Pioneer Square
stops.teaser: Seattle's original downtown, rebuilt in brick after a fire.
stops.map: Pioneer Square, 1st Ave S and Yesler Way, Seattle, WA
stops.clue: Walk to Occidental Park and Pioneer Place, where Yesler Way meets 1st Avenue, and find the iron-and-glass pergola.
stops.safety: The area is busy, with traffic and light rail nearby. Use crosswalks and watch for uneven brick sidewalks.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.hint: About 20 years after the great fire.
q.verify: Wikipedia says an iron and glass pergola designed by Julian F. Everett was added in 1909. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.line: First Avenue South in Pioneer Square in 1901.

now.head: Today
now.label: The park today
now.line: The pergola stands beside the totem pole.

story: Seattle's founders settled at Pioneer Square in 1852. Henry Yesler built a sawmill at the foot of what is now Yesler Way. The neighborhood was once known as Skid Road and Skid Row.

The Great Seattle Fire of June 6, 1889 destroyed Pioneer Square. By the end of 1890, dozens of brick and stone buildings in the Richardsonian Romanesque style had replaced the wood ones. The Seattle Underground Tour shows old storefronts buried when streets were raised.

In 1899, citizens stole a Tlingit totem pole and set it in Pioneer Place Park. They paid a $500 settlement. After an arsonist damaged it in 1938, a replacement was installed in 1940. The Pioneer Square-Skid Road Historic District was added to the National Register on June 22, 1970.
stops.fact: Citizens stole a totem pole in 1899 and paid a $500 settlement.
stops.disputed: The Wikipedia page for the neighborhood does not explain where the term Skid Road came from, so do not repeat popular origin stories without a source.

claims.t: A fire destroyed Pioneer Square in 1889.
Henry Yesler's sawmill was built after the 1889 fire.
claims.why: Yesler chose the site in 1852, before the fire.

spot.q: The 1901 photo shows brick buildings in Pioneer Square. What destroyed the old wooden district first?
options: The Great Seattle Fire of June 6, 1889
spot.why: The Great Seattle Fire of June 6, 1889 destroyed Pioneer Square. By the end of 1890, dozens of brick and stone buildings had replaced the wood ones.
